ambiguities.proposed_answer: 60 seconds, at the 99th percentile, measured from the API accepting the delete or report. This is achievable with active Redis invalidation plus a cache TTL capped at 60s. Note the number is load-bearing on the architecture, not cosmetic: a sub-second bound forces synchronous invalidation across every cache tier and rules out TTL-only safety nets, while a 5-minute bound would let us drop active invalidation entirely. The business owns this figure because it is the one quoted to fraud teams.
ambiguities.question: What is the published takedown time bound in AC9 — the specific number the business will be held to for a deleted or abuse-reported link to stop redirecting, measured from the delete/report?

ambiguities.proposed_answer: Define a ThreatCheck port with two implementations in this build: a Postgres-backed domain/URL denylist (synchronous, on the create path) and a no-op. Fail open on checker unavailability, consistent with AC20's preference for availability, and log it. No third-party reputation vendor is integrated, since none is named in the constraints and adding a paid external dependency on the create path is a procurement and latency decision, not an engineering one. Re-scanning already-issued links is handled by the takedown path (Q1), not by a background crawler. If a real reputation feed is expected in this build, that is a materially larger piece of work and the design must change.
ambiguities.question: AC21 requires that a phishing/malware URL never becomes a working link and that an existing link found to point at one stops redirecting. What decides that a URL is phishing or malware — an external reputation service (e.g. Google Safe Browsing), an internally maintained blocklist, or only inbound abuse reports? And if that source is unreachable at creation time, do we fail open (accept the link) or fail closed (refuse it)?

ambiguities.proposed_answer: Expiry is settable in the create request and additionally changeable via a narrow owner-scoped PATCH on the link that accepts only the expiry field. The target URL remains immutable, which is what 'editing a link' was excluded to protect. This satisfies AC11 literally without reopening link editing.
ambiguities.question: AC11 says a link's expiry can be 'set or changed' per link, but editing a link after creation is listed as out of scope. Is there an endpoint to change the expiry of an existing link, or does 'changed' only mean 'chosen per link at creation and adjustable in the database'?

ambiguities.proposed_answer: Yes — a report immediately transitions the link to a blocked state, per AC9, since no moderation console exists in this build. To keep that from being a trivial way to kill any competitor's link, reports require a signed-in session, are rate-limited per reporter, and the reporter id plus timestamp are recorded for the future review process. Flag for the reviewer: an open, unauthenticated report endpoint with automatic takedown would make the service self-weaponizable, so we are deliberately not building that.
ambiguities.question: AC9 implies that reporting a link as abusive stops it working within the SLA, but who may file a report and whether any human review intervenes are both out of scope. Does a single report immediately disable the link?

ambiguities.proposed_answer: The click is always served; counting is durable but not transactional with the redirect. Redis runs with AOF (appendfsync everysec) as the buffer and flushes to Postgres in batches, so counts survive process restart and Postgres outages, with at most a ~1s window at risk on catastrophic Redis node loss. AC20 already states the preference explicitly: serve the click. 'Exact' is read as 'measured, never sampled or estimated', not 'survives total infrastructure loss'.
ambiguities.question: AC3 requires exact click counts 'for the life of the link', while AC20 requires clicks to keep being served and counted during backend failure. If the counting store loses in-flight increments during an infrastructure failure, is a bounded count loss acceptable, or must a click that cannot be durably counted be refused?

ambiguities.proposed_answer: 302 for GET and HEAD; 405 for other methods. 302 is what every intermediary handles predictably and, with no-store headers, satisfies AC4. 307's method-preserving semantics are irrelevant because clicks are browser GETs.
ambiguities.question: Should the redirect be 302 or 307, and should non-GET methods on a short code be handled?

ambiguities.proposed_answer: Return both: the code and the fully-qualified short URL built from a configured base domain. Callers want a paste-ready URL, and keeping the code as a separate field means a future customer-owned-domain feature changes the URL field's host without breaking clients that key on the code.
ambiguities.question: What is returned in the create response — the bare code, or the full short URL — and where does the base domain come from?

ambiguities.proposed_answer: 24 hours, non-refreshable, no revocation list. Short enough that a leaked token has a bounded blast radius, long enough not to need refresh machinery that was not requested. The value is configuration, so it can be tightened without a code change.
ambiguities.question: How long is a session token valid, given that session lifetime, sign-out and revocation are all out of scope?

ambiguities.proposed_answer: No quota entity is modelled. Junk-link storage burn is handled purely by the per-customer create rate limit (A13), which is configuration. This keeps quotas out of the data model, as intake directed, while still satisfying AC19.
ambiguities.question: Is there a cap on how many links one customer may create, given that quotas and plan enforcement are out of scope but 'storage-burning junk links' is named as an attack to resist?

ambiguities.proposed_answer: Provide an owner-scoped, paginated list endpoint in addition to fetch-by-code. Without a UI, a customer who loses a code otherwise has no way to reach their own link, and the endpoint is owner-filtered so it creates no cross-tenant exposure.
ambiguities.question: Does listing a customer's own links fall under 'letting a customer see how a link has performed', or is retrieval only ever by known short code?

assumptions.rationale: AC4 forbids browsers/intermediaries short-circuiting us. 301 is cached indefinitely by default and would silently lose clicks; 302 plus explicit no-store headers is the standard way to force every click back to the service.
assumptions.statement: Redirects use HTTP 302 (GET/HEAD only) with Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, Pragma: no-cache and Expires: 0; 301 is never emitted.

assumptions.rationale: AC16 treats codes as secrets. Sequential or hash-derived codes are enumerable. 128 bits makes guessing at 100M links/day statistically hopeless while keeping the code short enough to be a usable short link.
assumptions.statement: Generated short codes are 128 bits of CSPRNG output rendered as ~11 base62 characters, with no derivation from row id, creation time, or the long URL; collisions are handled by a unique-constraint insert retry.

assumptions.rationale: A brand-readable alias is by definition guessable; AC5 and AC16 cannot both hold for customer-chosen strings. Sharing one namespace is required so AC6's collision rejection is meaningful. Reserved words prevent an alias shadowing an API route.
assumptions.statement: Customer-chosen aliases live in the same namespace as generated codes, restricted to [A-Za-z0-9_-]{3,64}, checked against a reserved-word list (api, health, admin, static, metrics, robots.txt, etc.), and AC16's unguessability guarantee is understood to apply only to codes we generate.

assumptions.rationale: AC13 and AC15 require indistinguishability. A 403/404 split leaks existence, which is exactly the enumeration oracle AC16 is trying to close.
assumptions.statement: Unknown, expired, deleted, blocked and other-customer codes all produce an identical 404 with an identical body on both the click path and the owner-scoped management endpoints; 403 is never returned for a link that exists but is not yours.

assumptions.rationale: AC18 forbids a per-request call to the login system, which rules out opaque tokens needing introspection. Asymmetric signing lets future services verify without holding the signing key. Sign-out and revocation are explicitly out of scope, so no denylist is built.
assumptions.statement: Sessions are stateless JWTs signed with an asymmetric key (EdDSA/RS256), verified locally against a published public key, with a 24-hour expiry and no revocation list.

assumptions.rationale: AC17 requires stolen-database resistance. A memory-hard KDF is the current baseline. A pepper adds key-management burden that the requirement never asks for and that breaks if the key is lost.
assumptions.statement: Passwords are hashed with Argon2id at OWASP-recommended parameters (bcrypt cost 12 as fallback if Argon2 is unavailable in the deployment image); no application-side pepper.

assumptions.rationale: AC10 says 'about a month'; 30 days is the least surprising reading. Per-row absolute timestamps satisfy AC11 (data-driven, not code change) and leave room for the future never-expiring paid tier as a NULL expires_at without a schema change.
assumptions.statement: Default link expiry is exactly 30 days from creation, stored as an absolute expires_at timestamp on each link row and overridable per link in the create request; there is no global compile-time constant.

assumptions.rationale: Intake put analytics beyond the click count out of scope. The count is the only performance figure the goal statement commits to.
assumptions.statement: 'How a link has performed' (AC7) returns exactly: short code/URL, long URL, created_at, expires_at, status, and total click count. No time series, referrer, geography, device or unique-visitor data.

assumptions.rationale: A synchronous Postgres write per click cannot hold at 1B clicks/day and violates AC20 (clicks must survive Postgres trouble). Summing the un-flushed delta at read time keeps AC7's 'reflects clicks already made' true rather than lagging by the flush interval.
assumptions.statement: Clicks increment a Redis counter on the hot path and are flushed to PostgreSQL asynchronously in batches; the reported count is the PostgreSQL total plus the un-flushed Redis delta.

assumptions.rationale: AC22's hot-link spike and AC20's 'clicks survive a degraded backend' both require the click path to avoid Postgres. Bounding TTL by the takedown SLA means a missed invalidation still cannot exceed the published AC9 number.
assumptions.statement: Code-to-URL resolution is served from a Redis cache (including negative caching of unknown codes) with Postgres consulted only on miss; cache entry TTL is set at or below the takedown SLA and entries are actively invalidated on delete, expiry and abuse takedown.

assumptions.rationale: A reissued code would silently redirect traffic from an old link's audience to a new owner's target — a security problem, not just a tidiness one. Data retention is out of scope, so rows are kept rather than purged.
assumptions.statement: Deletion is a soft delete (tombstone row retained, status flipped); codes are never reissued to another customer, and click counts of deleted links are retained.

assumptions.rationale: AC3's count is 'clicks made on it' for the life of the link; once the link is dead there is no redirect to attribute. Counting 404s would also let an attacker inflate a competitor's reported figures.
assumptions.statement: Clicks on deleted, expired or blocked links return 404 and are not added to the click count.

assumptions.rationale: AC19 names three distinct attacks — mining, existence scraping, bulk junk creation — which have different natural keys. Separating the 404 bucket is what actually stops enumeration without throttling legitimate high-volume clicking on a hot link (AC22).
assumptions.statement: Rate limiting is a Redis token bucket, keyed by client IP for the public click path (with a distinct, much tighter bucket for requests that 404, to catch enumeration) and by customer id for authenticated writes; over-limit returns 429 with Retry-After, and limits are configuration, not code.

assumptions.rationale: Blocks SSRF-flavoured abuse and self-referential redirect loops, and bounds the storage burn from junk-link attacks. 2048 is the pragmatic browser-compatible ceiling.
assumptions.statement: Submitted long URLs must be absolute http/https, at most 2048 characters, and are rejected if the host is a loopback, private, link-local or otherwise internal address, or the shortener's own domain.

assumptions.rationale: Keeps the click path free of a prefix and clear of API routes. Scoping uniqueness by domain now is a one-column decision that avoids a data migration when customer-owned domains arrive, which the constraints say must not be precluded.
assumptions.statement: Management endpoints are JSON under a versioned prefix (/api/v1/...) while the redirect lives at the root path /{code}; the public base URL for building returned short links is configuration, and code uniqueness is enforced on (domain, code) from day one with a single default domain.

assumptions.rationale: Roles, teams and multiple users per customer are out of scope. Modelling ownership on a customer id keeps a later user/team split additive.
assumptions.statement: One customer equals one login identity; 'customer' and 'user' are the same entity, and links are owned by that id.

assumptions.rationale: Deduplication would share a count across customers and leak that another customer already shortened that URL, breaking AC13's isolation.
assumptions.statement: The same long URL submitted twice yields two distinct short links with independent counts.

assumptions.rationale: Intake puts provisioning out of scope while AC12/AC17/AC18 require us to hold credentials and issue sessions. Seeding is the smallest thing that makes the system testable without building a sign-up flow nobody asked for.
assumptions.statement: Customer accounts are seeded by database migration/fixture for this build; no public registration endpoint is exposed, but a sign-in endpoint issuing the session token is in scope.
